newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Clinton says Bosnia arrests were "right thing".
newsitem.headline: Clinton says Bosnia arrests were "right thing".

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Friday he had no reports of disturbances in Bosnia after NATO's sudden swoop on Bosnian Serb war crimes suspects, and defended the action as "the right thing to do".

Asked whether situation was calm after British peacekeeping forces arrested one suspect on Thursday and shot dead another, Clinton told reporters during a visit to Bucharest: "So far yes. We have no reports to the contrary."
"I think what was done was appropriate and within the SFOR mandate," Clinton said, referring to the NATO-led stabilisation force in Bosnia. "I think it was the right thing to do."

But as Clinton defended the move, Russia strongly condemned it. A foreign ministry statement in Moscow said such "cowboy" raids endangered the peace process in Bosnia and the Russian leadership would draw "corresponding conclusions" from them.
Russia, which has a long-standing sympathy for the Serbs, contributes to the 31,000-strong Bosnia peacekeeping force.

In the first NATO operation against indicted war criminals since a Bosnia peace treaty was signed in 1995, Simo Drljaca, a Bosnian Serb police chief, was killed when he opened fire on soldiers trying to arrest him in the northwest Prijedor region.
Milan Kovacevic, a hospital director, was captured at work and flown to The Hague to face trial before the United Nations war crimes tribunal. The NATO action has shocked Bosnian Serb leaders.

Clinton, speaking before talks with Romanian President Emil Constantinescu, noted that Drljaca and Kovacevic were under sealed indictment from the Hague tribunal and had come in regular contact with SFOR forces.
The SFOR mandate allows forces to arrest war crimes suspects with whom they come in contact, but not to engage in manhunts.

U.S. officials said on Thursday that U.S. troops in SFOR had given logistical support to the British operation but had not taken a direct part in it. Clinton was briefed last week about the plan, they said.
The State Department has warned Americans to be cautious if travelling in Serbia and Montenegro, saying the arrests might spark tensions in former Yugoslavia.
